newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch IGC delegate sees firm move by EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Dutch IGC delegate sees firm move by EU summit.

text.p: The man who will steer the inter-governmental conference (IGC) towards the finish line next year says negotiations are moving along at a reasonable rate but that EU leaders want to make sure it stays that way.
Dutch European Affairs Minister Michiel Patijn said in an interview with Reuters this week that it was no surprise that the IGC had not shown much tangible progress.
"If you schedule a conference for 15 months, you cannot expect much to happen in the very first five months, he said.
But the final treaty, expected to be agreed sometime in the middle of next year, was taking shape.
"There are contours of what will be coming," Patijn said.
He said it was clear there would be a strengthening of the institutional framework and that language on employment would also be included in the new treaty.
Patijn, the Dutch delegate to the EU foreign ministers' representatives group, will take over chairing the negotiations in January when the Netherlands's EU presidency begins.
Plans call for the IGC to end and a new treaty to be agreed by the end of the presidency -- although it is admitted that the negotiations could carry over into the Luxembourg presidency.
Although agreements will ultimately be decided in national capitals, it will be Patijn's brief to ensure that the treaty writing and nitty-gritty negotiating runs smoothly.
So far things were going according to plan, he said.
The Irish European Union presidency was organising the IGC well and there would be a draft treaty ready for Dublin II, the December European Council.
"The Irish are doing a reasonably good job," Patijn said. "They have set out a clear schedule for how they are going to work in the second semester"
As for the draft treaty, ordered by EU leaders at the Florence European Council: "It will be a paper with a lot of brackets but that is because it is early (in the negotiations)."
Not everyone, of course, is publicly persuaded that the IGC is moving apace, which is why, urged on by French President Jacques Chirac, EU leaders plan a summit in Dublin on October 5.
Critics have charged that the IGC has deteriorated into a seemingly endless roundtable discussion of what each member state wants.

British objections to new integration and the hesitancy of others to commit to compromises while the current British government remain in office have been blamed for some of the IGC's lack of agreement.
But Patijn said member states had to start reaching deals to keep the IGC on schedule.
"There is a kind of observers' widsom that nothing will happen until the British elections (next spring). That kind of thinking has be rejected," he said.

Participants argue that the negotiations have actually moved further than conventional wisdom would have it, noting that each week the representatives' meeting goes over proposed texts rather than just a wishlist.
However, EU leaders are keen to persuade the public both that the IGC is moving along and that it is essential for the bloc's future.
Patijn said he expected this would be the message from the one-day informal summit next week.

"What I expect to come out of it is a sense of determination and a strong sense of urgency from the European Council," he said, adding that the leaders would stress "the importance of a substantive and timely result for the conference".
He said it should allow the member states to see where the stand.
"Do we still agree on the political objectives? Do we still agree on the role the conference plays in the larger political and institutional decisions that have to be taken?" he said.
Patijn said finishing the IGC was clearly the Dutch EU presidency main priority, but that it would not be the sole focus.

"We consider our presidency as a part of a continuum. We have a host of other difficulties to handle," he said, referring to preparations for economic and monetary union (EMU), future financing and the planned enlargement.
Patijn said the Dutch would not, of course, conclude any of the projects except the IGC, but that would not stop them working hard on them.
"At least we have to make an indent," he said.
